Eye bars V. 26.1 2/9

1. Implementation

The document has been created and approved by the General Assembly of 09.11.2024.
The document and its rules have been implemented since the 2025 season.

2. Definition and Description

2.1. Definition

“Eye bars” are the term used to describe additional protection for the eye slots of a helmet.
Rare historical sources display some additional eye protection, mainly for great helms.

However, it is permitted to add Eye bars that do not rely on historical sources to increase the safety of
helmets. The number and type of permitted Eye bars are displayed in each helmet rules document.

2.2. Eye bars Description

Eye bars can be:

● Externally Riveted Eye bars
This type of Eye bars is documented by historical sources for specific helmets. Therefore, they are
only allowed on helmet models that can be historically referenced to have externally riveted Eye
bars. If there is no supporting evidence for a particular helmet style, externally riveted Eye bars are
not permitted on that helmet.

● Integrated Eye bars
This type of Eye bars is documented by historical sources for certain helmets as part of the visor or
faceplate itself. They are only permitted on helmet models that can be shown to have used
integrated Eye bars historically. If no suitable source exists, integrated Eye bars are not allowed.
They must closely replicate the shape, placement, and size seen in surviving artifacts or credible
period art.

● Safety Eye bars
This type of Eye bar is not documented by historical sources. These concealed Eye bars are
allowed solely to increase safety in modern buhurt combat. They typically consist of metal bars
riveted or welded to the inside of a helmet, thus remaining concealed from the outside.

Number and Placement of Safety Eye bars:

○ For helmets with two separate Eye slots, you may install up to two (2) vertical
Eye bars per Eye slot.

○ For helmets with one continuous Eye slot, you may install up to five (5) Eye bars
across the slot.

3. General Requirements

All types of Eye bars must respect the following requirements:
● Be firmly attached to prevent any breakage and maintain a high level of protection in any situation.

● Protect the whole Eye slot from top to bottom.

Recommended: Eye slots should not exceed an opening of 25 mm

<< 25mm tall maximum |

4. Externally Riveted Eye bars

4.1. Historical Sources and Datation

A few historical sources display this type of Eye bar.
The main source is the Great Helm from Nuremberg (1350).

Despite its rarity, it is Approved for 14th century, Transitional and 15th century armors.

4.2. Specific Requirements

Externally riveted Eye bars must:
● conform with the General Requirements (see Section 3 above),
● be firmly riveted to the outside of the Eye slot,
● resemble the historical sources and not exceed a width of 30mm,
● be made of metal.

example. .

5.2. Specific Requirements

Integrated Eye bars must:
● conform with the general requirements (see Section 3 above),
● be sturdy made and able to endure full-contact fights,
● resemble the historical sources and not exceed a width of 20mm.

6. Safety Eye bars

6.1. Historical Sources and Datation

There are no historical sources for Eye bars welded onto Eye slots.

Nevertheless, for safety reasons, they are Approved for 14th century, Transitional and 15th century
armors.

6.2. Specific Requirements

Safety Eye bars must:

● conform with the General Requirements (see Section 3 above),
● be welded or riveted from the inside of the helm,

● be sturdy made and able to endure full-contact fights,

● be painted black.

6.3. Examples of Approved Reproductions
